body_text:
The Identity Theorem and Isolated Zeros.

Let $U \subseteq \mathbb{C}$ be a connected open domain and let $f, g: U \to \mathbb{C}$ be holomorphic.
If the coincidence set $S = \{z \in U : f(z) = g(z)\}$ has an accumulation point in $U$, then:
$$ f(z) = g(z) \quad \text{for all } z \in U. $$

*Consequence (Isolated Zeros)*: If $f$ is a non-zero holomorphic function on a connected domain $U$,
then its zero set $Z(f) = \{z \in U : f(z) = 0\}$ has no accumulation points in $U$; that is, every zero
is isolated. Near any zero $z_0 \in Z(f)$, there exists an integer $m \ge 1$ (the *order* or *multiplicity*)
and a holomorphic function $h$ with $h(z_0) \ne 0$ such that $f(z) = (z - z_0)^m h(z)$.

*Proof of the Identity Theorem*: Consider the difference function $h = f - g$. Let $z_0 \in U$ be an
accumulation point of zeros of $h$. By continuity, $h(z_0) = 0$. Expand $h$ into its Taylor series
$h(z) = \sum_{n=0}^\infty a_n (z - z_0)^n$ on a disk $D(z_0, r) \subseteq U$.
If not all $a_n$ were zero, let $a_m$ be the first non-zero coefficient ($m \ge 1$):
$$ h(z) = (z - z_0)^m [a_m + a_{m+1}(z - z_0) + \cdots] = (z - z_0)^m \psi(z), $$
where $\psi(z_0) = a_m \ne 0$. By continuity, $\psi(z) \ne 0$ in some punctured disk $D^*(z_0, \delta)$.
Thus $h(z) \ne 0$ for all $0 < |z - z_0| < \delta$, contradicting the assumption that $z_0$ is an
accumulation point of zeros. Hence all $a_n = 0$, so $h$ vanishes identically on $D(z_0, r)$.
Defining $A \subseteq U$ to be the set of points where all derivatives $h^{(n)}$ vanish, $A$ is both
open (by Taylor expansion) and closed in $U$ (by continuity of derivatives). Since $U$ is connected and
$A$ is nonempty, $A = U$, so $h \equiv 0$ on all of $U$.
